beats.narration_text: Ciao — this is Liam. Episode 4 of 6. You named the thing in /v0. Now you build the SDD. Gru has five command families — Problem and Vision, Systems, Domain and API, Scope and Production, and Compile. Each family is a phase. Each phase gate requires the previous one to pass. This episode maps every command family, walks the phase sequence, and shows Gru's pushback layer in action on a real example. Seven minutes. This is the engine room.

props.topic: WHAT IS GRU? — E4/6: COMMAND LIBRARY + PHASE GATES
props.segment: Build the SDD: The Command Library and Phase Gates
props.command: Gru session with /v0 already passed. Run /v1 to begin the Problem & Vision phase.
props.runningText: five command families — fixed sequence — phase gate at each boundary — pushback on by default…
output: Problem & Vision: /v1 intake / /v2 principles / /v3 flows / /v4 needs

beats.narration_text: The first command family is Problem and Vision — four commands in sequence. /v1 is the intake. You tell Gru who the users are, what the current state of the system is, and what the failure mode looks like if the system does not exist. Gru summarizes this into a problem statement and checks it against your /v0 naming. If they conflict, Gru flags it. /v2 is principles. You define the design principles the system must honor — performance constraints, correctness requirements, the non-negotiables. These become the standard against which every later decision is measured. If a later command proposes something that violates a /v2 principle, Gru will call it out. /v3 is flows. You map the data flows and user journeys the system participates in — what enters, what exits, in what sequence. This is where the insertion point you named in /v0 becomes a concrete diagram. /v4 is needs. You derive the functional requirements — the specific behaviors the system must exhibit to fulfill the flows, consistent with the principles. Every need statement must trace back to a flow. A need with no flow is a feature that was not designed — and Gru will ask you to justify it.

lines: The first phase: from intake to derived needs
/v1 Intake: users + current state + failure mode / problem
/v2 Principles: non-negotiables — performance, correctness, design constraints. Violations flagged later.

beats.narration_text: The second family is Systems — /s1 through /s4. /s1 is the component map: you list every component in the system, name it, describe its responsibility, and map it to one or more Needs from /v4. A component that maps to no Need is a component that was not designed — and Gru will flag it. /s2 is the data model: every entity, its fields, its types, and the invariants that must hold. /s3 is the integration map: how the system connects to external services, APIs, and data sources — each connection with a failure mode. /s4 is the state model: what states the system can be in, what transitions are valid, and what events drive them. The third family is Domain and API — /d1 through /d3. /d1 is the domain glossary: every domain term used in the SDD is defined precisely so that a new engineer could read the document without domain background. /d2 is the API contract: every endpoint or interface the system exposes, with its inputs, outputs, and error conditions. /d3 is the data contract: the exact schema of every artifact the system produces — the typed output you promised in /v0. If the schema here does not match the /v0 output, Gru catches the inconsistency.

lines: /s1 Component map: every component named, responsibility, mapped to a /v4 Need
/s2 Data model: entities, fields, types, invariants.

beats.act: Scope and Production — /p1-/p5 — and the pushback layer
beats.narration_text: The fourth family is Scope and Production — /p1 through /p5. /p1 is the scope boundary: what the system explicitly does and does not do. The 'does not do' list is as important as the 'does' list — every feature you leave out of scope is a handoff condition the Boondoggle Score will verify later. /p2 is the testing strategy: how you verify that each Need is met, including the edge cases and the domain-specific failure modes /g2 will probe. /p3 is the deployment plan: how the system gets to production and what the rollback procedure is. /p4 is the observability plan: what you log, what you monitor, and what an alert looks like. /p5 is the risk register: every assumption the SDD makes, ranked by impact if wrong. Now, the pushback layer. At every phase, Gru is running in constructive-skeptic mode. It flags weak input — a need statement that is too vague to implement, a principle that contradicts a flow, an assumption in /p5 that was never surfaced. It names assumptions you did not articulate. It disagrees when a decision in a later phase contradicts a principle you set in /v2. This is the mode you should stay in. /silent turns it off. Do not use /silent until you have already run the full sequence in interactive mode at least once.

lines: /p1 Scope boundary: does + does NOT do
/p2 Testing strategy: per-Need verification + domain-specific failure modes.

beats.act: Compile and audits — /g1, /g2, /g4 — and the demo
beats.narration_text: The final family is Compile. /g1 compiles the full Software Design Document from everything you have built across the phase sequence. It is a synthesis, not a generation — it assembles your inputs into a single coherent document and surfaces any internal inconsistencies it finds. /g2 is the failure-mode audit. It runs the seven failure modes against your SDD — the seven ways an AI system most commonly ships wrong in production. You get one finding per failure mode, with a severity level and a specific recommendation. /g4 is the new-engineer test: Gru generates three questions a new engineer would ask if handed your SDD on day one. If the SDD cannot answer those questions, there are holes in the document. Now the demo — I run /v1 on the Invoice Integrity Checker from Episode 3, and show what real pushback looks like. I tell Gru the users are finance clerks who process invoices daily. Gru immediately asks: are the clerks the ones who resolve flags, or does a separate approval step exist? That question is not pedantic — it changes the state model in /s4 and the observability requirements in /p4. That is the pushback layer doing its job.

beats.narration_text: One more thing on /silent, because students misuse it. Silent mode produces clean output — no pushback, no clarifying questions, no flags. It is designed for practitioners who are running a known workflow and don't need Gru to probe their decisions. For a student on a first Boondoggle Report, that is almost never you. The trap is using /silent to skip a gate you are stuck on. Specifically: using /silent on /v2 because you cannot articulate your principles. Using /silent on /p5 because you cannot name your assumptions. If you cannot articulate them interactively, you have not thought them through — and the score will expose that later. There is one valid use of /silent before you complete the full interactive sequence: if you have already run /v0 through /v4 in interactive mode and you want a clean version of the same output for a document, /silent on /g1 is reasonable. That is the only case. The rule: silent mode is for when you already know. It is not for skipping the knowing.

lines: Silent mode is for when you already know
/silent: clean output, no pushback, no flags
Trap #1: /silent on /v2 because you can't articulate your principles. Don't.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for Build the SDD: Command Library and Phase Gates. Five families in sequence. Problem and Vision: /v1 intake, /v2 principles, /v3 flows, /v4 needs — every need must trace to a flow. Systems: /s1 component map, /s2 data model, /s3 integrations, /s4 state model — every component must map to a need. Domain and API: /d1 glossary, /d2 API contract, /d3 data contract — schema must match the /v0 output promise. Scope and Production: /p1 scope boundary, /p2 testing, /p3 deployment, /p4 observability, /p5 risk register. Compile: /g1 SDD, /g2 seven failure modes, /g4 new-engineer test. Pushback layer is on by default — stay in interactive mode through at least one full run. /silent is for practitioners, not for skipping gates.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt — paste it into your Gru session after /v0 has passed. The prompt reads: I am ready to begin building the SDD. My /v0 is: [paste your passed /v0 sentence here]. Run /v1. Ask me every clarifying question you would need to write a complete problem statement. End quote. When Gru pushes back on any answer, do not rephrase the same answer more slowly. Address the specific thing Gru named. If Gru asks whether the users who trigger the system are the same users who review its output — that is an architectural question disguised as a UX question. Answer it architecturally. Run /v1, get through the pushback, and stop there. You do not need to finish /v2 today. The habit this episode is building is: one gate, fully, before the next one opens. The students who skip phases are the same ones who get a Boondoggle Score with a zero-PA distribution. They built without auditing. The score finds it.
